# Voorzetselpaden — image plan, A0–A2

Status: delivered 10 November 2026. This is the first of six image
plans: **A0–A2** (this file), then A2 pairs (4b), A2+, B1, B1+ and B2. It
covers the new frames in
batch 4 of `prepositions-roadmap.md` only. All twenty images below are drawn,
processed and in the game data; the prompts stay here as the record.

The thirty pilot scenes already exist in `assets/voorzetselpaden/` and are
listed in `prepositions-art.md`. **Do not redraw them.** Everything below is a
frame the game does not have yet.

Batch 4 is the A2 slice of phase A. Batches 5–8 (spatial set, adjective and noun
chunks, pronominals) open the A2+ band and belong in `prepositions-art-a2-plus.md`;
the B1, B1+ and B2 bands follow in `prepositions-art-b1.md`,
`prepositions-art-b1-plus.md` and `prepositions-art-b2.md`.

With the thirty pilot scenes, these twenty complete the A0–A2 band at fifty
frames. Nothing else in A0–A2 is missing. A later appendix proposes three
variant scenes for each of those fifty frames; it is a proposal only and does
not change this delivered set. See *Appendix — three extra scenes per frame* at
the end of this file.

A smaller follow-on batch, **4b**, is drawn in
`prepositions-art-a2-pairs.md`: sixteen frames that give existing singles a
contrast partner, plus two same-verb pairs and one lone single. It introduces
no new preposition. This file remains the record of the fifty delivered frames;
do not add 4b rows here.

## How to use this file

Each numbered section is a self-contained prompt. Paste the whole fenced block
into Grok, one block at a time. Grok has no file access, so nothing outside the
block is assumed. Ask for each prompt's ten images, then process the result as
described in `game-art.md` under *Delivered raster art* and ship at 512 × 763.

The house style is the bold brush-pen sketch defined in `game-art.md`: cobalt
`#2B50C8` only, wide-nib contour with directional hatching, 2:3 portrait, one
idea per image, no text. The prompts repeat those rules because the generator
cannot read `game-art.md`.

## What batch 4 adds

Twenty frames around the batch-4 prepositions `tegen`, `door` and `uit`, with
supporting `aan`, `met`, `op`, `in` and `voor` frames. Four are contrast pairs
that must be drawn together; the rest are singles. `zonder` and `tot` are
deliberately not framed: see the note under the table.

`zonder` and `tot` are deliberately absent.

- `zonder + noun` (`zonder afspraak`, `zonder moeite`) is free prepositional use
  and just means "without + the noun", so it teaches the word `zonder`, not a
  chunk. `prepositions-roadmap.md` §11 rules this out of the frame set. Items
  14–17 therefore use real verb/adjective + preposition chunks instead: `letten
  op`, `bezig zijn met`, `geïnteresseerd zijn in`, `tevreden zijn met`.
- `tot ziens` and `tot morgen` are farewell formulae and `tot nu toe` is a fixed
  adverbial; in none of the three does a verb, adjective or noun select `tot`.
  Items 18–20 are therefore real frames with a governed preposition: `bedanken
  voor`, `feliciteren met`, `uitnodigen voor`.

## Appendix — three extra scenes per frame (proposal, not delivered)

Added 10 November 2026. This appendix does **not** change the delivered fifty
or the status of batch 4. It proposes three further scenes for every A0–A2
frame, so each chunk has four exemplars instead of one. Nothing here is drawn,
promoted or in `prepositions.json`; every row is `planned`.

### Recommendation

Why three and not one or two: one scene teaches recognition of that scene, not
the chunk. Two gives a contrast but still lets the learner memorise a single
pairing. Four different situations force the preposition to carry the meaning
across contexts. The contrast pairs benefit most, because the learner must keep
`op` and `voor`, `aan` and `over`, `met` and `tegen` apart when the setting
changes.

### Engine implication (for whoever codes this)

`prepositions.json` currently stores one `scene` string per frame. These 150
files cannot be used by adding them to `scenes` alone: the engine needs to know
which frame each variant belongs to, choose one variant per session, and never
offer two variants of the same frame as Kies options, because both would be
correct. The Klopt stop also needs the scene's frame. This is a schema and
engine change, not an art drop. Do not promote these files until that is
decided.

### The 150 scenes

All rows are planned. The cross-check column names the nearest confusion to
avoid; the prompt for each batch repeats it in full.

### Delivery for this appendix

1. Do not mark a row `drawn` until the PNG is processed to alpha at 512 × 763
   and the scene is in `prepositions.json`.
2. Keep the file name exact. `eraan-denken-*` are Ontdek-only cards for the
   `denken` level, not scored frames; do not give them a `contrast`.
3. The 150 rows are grouped into the fourteen prompts below. Draw each prompt
   in one sitting so the cross-checks are done on the same figures and camera.
4. After promotion, update the engine as described under *Engine implication*
   before the extra scenes can appear in a session.

## Redraw pass — the anchors are locked

The art set now has three generations in it, not two:

The third is the target. `game-art.md` now describes it and carries the locked
header; this section is only the work order.

### What actually needs redrawing

The sixteen covered frames are `bedanken voor`, `bezig zijn met`, `denken aan`,
`denken over`, `doorbrengen met`, `drinken uit`, `eraan denken`,
`feliciteren met`, `geïnteresseerd in`, `letten op`, `stappen uit`,
`tevreden zijn met`, `uitnodigen voor`, `vallen uit`, `wachten op` and
`wachten voor`. Each still has its old shipped file (`wachten-op-bus.png`,
`drinken-uit-glas.png`, …) wired into `prepositions.json` while the new variant
sits in the archived `incoming/` folder. That is a **data decision, not an art
job**: either the frame keeps the old scene and gets redrawn after all, or the
engine repoints to the new variant and the old file is retired. Do not redraw
these until that is settled.

### Batching

Five per batch, following the contrast families so a pair is never split. Batch
R1 is deliberately four images: it is the test that decides whether the header
works.

All filenames are `<chunk>-<object>.png` in the folder they already live in.
Deliver each redraw as `<name>-v2.png` so the old file survives for comparison;
renaming happens at integration, not at generation.

Scene sources for the wording: `prepositions-art-prompts.md` (batches 1–3, the
full `Scene / Must read / Avoid` form), the batch-4 table above, and
`prepositions-art-a2-pairs.md` for batch 4b. Translate each one the way R1 was
translated — same meaning, no cartoon vocabulary.

### How a redraw batch is phrased

Grok gets a fresh context about every ten images, so nothing survives between
sessions except what is inside the paste block. Two consequences:

- **Never attach the old drawing.** The old files are cartoon, solid-filled and
dot-eyed; attaching one in a fresh context invites a traced copy of exactly
what we are removing, and nothing in that context would tell Grok it is a
before-picture. Describe the scene in words instead.
- **Every block carries the whole brief** — header, filenames, scenes, pair
checks, validation. Nothing may be left to an earlier message.

One block is pasted with the three anchors attached: the locked header from
`game-art.md`, then one batch block. One block per fresh context, five images
(R1 is four). Two blocks can share a context, but the line weight creeps by
image ten, so five is the safe number.

The briefs below are the old ones translated into the new visual language. The
meaning and the confusions are unchanged; "delighted", "scowling", "hands
raised" and "the gift is the main mass" are gone, because they describe the
cartoon. What replaces them is posture, eye line and which mark is clearest.

`R1` is the test batch. Continue to `R2` only if all four pass beside the
anchors at full size and at 64 px.

The ten paste-ready blocks are in `prepositions-art-redraw-prompts.md`: the
locked header once, then R1–R10. Each block is self-contained apart from the
header, and the header is re-pasted after every context reset.

# Voorzetselpaden — scene art

Pilot art briefs. The activity spec is `prepositions.md`; the code is
`prepositions-implementation.md`. The first ten images were enough to test the
meaning-first loop end to end; batches 2–4 take the set to fifty scenes and
thirty-three levels. Batch 4b is planned and would take it to sixty-seven
scenes and thirty-six levels.

The shared drawing rules are in `game-art.md`. This file lists what each scene
must show; that file says how it must be drawn. The generation prompts for each
batch are in `prepositions-art-prompts.md`.

Status: fifty images are drawn and in place — the first ten (batch 1), the next
ten (batch 2), the last ten of the pilot (batch 3) and the twenty A0–A2 frames
of batch 4. All fifty match their briefs.
Batch 3 is drawn with heavier, more solid masses than batches 1–2 and is not
literally in the brush line of the first set; it still reads at 64 px and no
scene was redrawn for it. Two batch-1 images are weaker and worth a redraw:
`denken-aan-persoon` reads as a portrait rather than a full scene, and
`eraan-denken-afspraak` has no cue that clearly separates it from `denken aan`
— the pair is meant to test the pronominal form, not a meaning contrast, so it
should not compete with the thought-bubble image.

Batch 4 is recorded in `prepositions-art-a0-a2.md`: twenty A0–A2 frames around
`tegen`, `door`, `uit` and `tot`, with supporting `aan`, `met`, `op` and `in`
frames. `zonder` is left out because `zonder + noun` is free prepositional use,
not a chunk. The later bands are in `prepositions-art-a2-plus.md` (A2+),
`prepositions-art-b1.md` (B1), `prepositions-art-b1-plus.md` (B1+) and
`prepositions-art-b2.md` (B2). All fifty scenes below are delivered; do not redraw
them.

Batch 4b is **drawn, not yet integrated**: sixteen frames that give existing
singles a partner and add two same-verb pairs plus one lone single. Its briefs
and prompts are in `prepositions-art-a2-pairs.md`. This file records only the
level composition, which that file decides.

## Where the files go

`assets/voorzetselpaden/<scene-id>.png`. Square was the plan; the delivered
set is portrait and is kept at that ratio so all fifty share one camera and one
scale — which matters most for the contrast pairs. Batch 1 arrived at
784 × 1168, batches 2 and 3 at 1152 × 1712, batch 4 mostly at 784 × 1168 with
`vallen-uit-tas` at 1152 × 1712; all ship at 512 × 763. See
"Delivered raster art" in `game-art.md` for how the files are prepared and drawn.
The untouched originals of batch 4 are in
`assets/verb-propositions/archived/04-a0-a2/`; the folder is grouped by batch,
see its `README.md`.

## Rules for every image

## The frame rule (all six plans)

A frame must be a chunk that governs a preposition — a verb (`letten op`), an
adjective (`bang voor`), a noun (`zin in`) or a fixed idiom. Not a bare verb,
not a free adjunct (`zonder afspraak`), not a greeting (`tot ziens`). A
pronominal adverb counts, because it carries its preposition inside `er…`,
`daar…` or `waar…` (`erover nadenken`, `ergens naartoe`, `ergens klaar mee
zijn`); the roadmap budgets 40 such frames.

Beyond the pilot, the plans are `prepositions-art-a0-a2.md` (20 frames),
`prepositions-art-a2-pairs.md` (16), `prepositions-art-a2-plus.md` (80),
`prepositions-art-b1.md` (120), `prepositions-art-b1-plus.md` (250) and
`prepositions-art-b2.md` (210): 696 new frames, 726 with the thirty pilot
scenes.

When editing a plan:

- Keep the tracker row and its batch subject identical — both filename and
  chunk. A plan breaks when only one side is updated.
- Batch prompts use four-backtick fences; an unbalanced fence silently breaks
  the copy-paste block.
- Filenames are ASCII; chunk text keeps its diacritics. No duplicate filenames
  and no duplicate Scene cells.
- A “has a preposition?” scan is clean once `tegenover` and the pronominal forms
  are whitelisted.

The audit that established this, and the scripts to re-run the checks, are in
`archive/preposition-review-findings-2026-11-10.md`.

## The first ten

## Briefs — batch 1

### 1. `wachten-op-bus.svg`

**Scene.** One person at a simple bus stop, body angled toward the road, looking
at a watch or phone. A pole with a blank sign (no text), maybe a bench.

**Must read at 64 px.** Waiting; a bus stop; for a bus.

**Avoid.** A bus arriving or a person boarding — that shows the event, not the
waiting. Avoid a queue, which suggests waiting in line rather than waiting for a
vehicle.

**Supports.** `Ik wacht op de bus.` / `Wachten op de bus.`

**Contrast.** `wachten-voor-deur`. This is the idiomatic "wait for", not the
spatial "wait in front of".

**Mode.** Ontdek, Kies het beeld, Klopt de zin?, Bouw de zin.

### 2. `wachten-voor-deur.svg`

**Scene.** One person standing outside a closed door, arms crossed or leaning
against the wall, clearly waiting. A plain door with a handle and a blank
nameplate (no text), maybe a doormat. The person is outside, not inside.

**Must read at 64 px.** Waiting; in front of a door.

**Avoid.** A bus stop, a person walking through the door, a key in hand (that
suggests entering, not waiting). Avoid a queue.

**Supports.** `Ik wacht voor de deur.` / `Wachten voor de deur.`

**Contrast.** `wachten-op-bus`. This is the spatial "in front of", not the
idiomatic "wait for". It exists to make the `op` in `wachten op` visible.

**Mode.** Ontdek, Kies het beeld, Klopt de zin?, Bouw de zin.

### 3. `denken-aan-persoon.svg`

**Scene.** A person sitting or standing still, gazing into space, with a thought
bubble containing a simple face (a friend or partner). Maybe a phone in hand, but
the face is in the thought bubble, not on the screen.

**Must read at 64 px.** Thinking of a person.

**Avoid.** A speech bubble (that is talking), two options or a question mark
(that is `denken over`), a calendar with a reminder (that is `eraan denken`).

**Supports.** `Ik denk aan jou.` / `Ik denk aan mijn vriend.`

**Contrast.** `denken-over-keuze`.

**Mode.** Ontdek, Kies het beeld, Klopt de zin?, Bouw de zin.

### 4. `denken-over-keuze.svg`

**Scene.** A person at a table with two simple options side by side — two house
shapes, two holiday photos, or two paths. Hand on chin, comparing. The options
are objects, not people.

**Must read at 64 px.** Considering a choice.

**Avoid.** A thought bubble containing a person (that is `denken aan`), a
question mark alone (too vague), a speech bubble.

**Supports.** `Ik denk over de keuze.` / `We denken over het plan.`

**Contrast.** `denken-aan-persoon`.

**Mode.** Ontdek, Kies het beeld, Klopt de zin?, Bouw de zin.

### 5. `uitkijken-naar-vakantie.svg`

**Scene.** A person with a suitcase, smiling, looking at a wall calendar with one
day circled and a sun or plane icon. No numbers or letters: use a blank grid with
one marked square.

**Must read at 64 px.** Looking forward to a future holiday.

**Avoid.** A bus or plane actually leaving (that is departure, not anticipation),
a warning gesture, a sad face.

**Supports.** `Ik kijk uit naar de vakantie.` / `We kijken uit naar de zomer.`

**Contrast.** `uitkijken-voor-auto`.

**Mode.** All four, including Bouw de zin. This is the main separable example:
`uit` belongs at the end.

### 6. `uitkijken-voor-auto.svg`

**Scene.** A child at the edge of a road, a car approaching, an adult hand
pulling the child back or an adult making a warning gesture. A simple warning
triangle without text can sit in the scene if it does not become the main idea.

**Must read at 64 px.** Danger; watch out.

**Avoid.** A happy person looking at a car (that is `uitkijken naar`), a bus stop,
a traffic light with text.

**Supports.** `Kijk uit voor de auto!` / `We moeten uitkijken voor het verkeer.`

**Contrast.** `uitkijken-naar-vakantie`.

**Mode.** All four. This is the second half of the `uitkijken` contrast and a
second split example.

### 7. `praten-met-vriend.svg`

**Scene.** Two people facing each other, both with speech bubbles that meet or
overlap, relaxed posture. Maybe a table between them, but no object that is the
topic of the conversation.

**Must read at 64 px.** A conversation with someone.

**Avoid.** One person alone, a phone (that is `bellen`), a house or object
between them (that is `praten over`).

**Supports.** `Ik praat met mijn vriend.` / `Zij praat met de buurman.`

**Contrast.** `praten-over-huis`.

**Mode.** Ontdek, Kies het beeld, Klopt de zin?, Bouw de zin.

### 8. `praten-over-huis.svg`

**Scene.** Two people at a table with a house, a photo of a house or a simple
blueprint between them. Speech bubbles point at the house; one person gestures
toward it.

**Must read at 64 px.** Talking about a topic or object.

**Avoid.** Two people just facing each other with no topic (that is
`praten met`), a person alone, a phone.

**Supports.** `We praten over het huis.` / `Zij praten over de plannen.`

**Contrast.** `praten-met-vriend`.

**Mode.** Ontdek, Kies het beeld, Klopt de zin?, Bouw de zin.

### 9. `ophouden-met-roken.svg`

**Scene.** A person stubbing out a cigarette in an ashtray, or holding up a hand
to refuse a cigarette, calm and determined. A packet of cigarettes can be put
away, but with no branding or text. A crossed-out cigarette symbol is allowed if
it stays wordless.

**Must read at 64 px.** Stopping smoking.

**Avoid.** A person smoking happily (that is the opposite), a "no smoking" sign
with letters, a doctor or a lecture.

**Supports.** `Ik hou op met roken.` / `Zij houdt op met roken.`

**Contrast.** None in the pilot. Use it in Ontdek, Kies het beeld and Bouw de
zin; skip `Klopt de zin?` until it has a partner.

**Note.** `ophouden` is separable, so `op` goes to the end. This is a second
split example beyond `uitkijken`, and it does not repeat the same prefix.

### 10. `eraan-denken-afspraak.svg`

**Scene.** A person with a hand to the forehead or a raised finger, sudden
recall. A phone or calendar with a bell or reminder icon nearby; maybe a clock.
No text or numbers.

**Must read at 64 px.** Remembering an appointment, "oh, I must remember".

**Avoid.** A thought bubble containing a person (that is `denken aan`), two
options or a question mark (that is `denken over`), a speech bubble.

**Supports.** `Ik denk eraan.` / `Ik moet eraan denken.` It also supports
`Ik denk aan de afspraak.`

**Related form.** `denken aan`, same meaning, pronoun form. This is not a meaning
contrast; it is the pronominal transformation.

**Mode.** Ontdek, Klopt de zin?, Hetzelfde of anders?, Krimp and the pronominal
step of Bouw de zin.

## Review sheet

`tools/build-prepositions-sheet.py` renders every frame in
`prepositions.json` — image, chunk, gloss, example (NL/EN), build sentences,
concept question and contrast partner — to
`assets/site/prepositions-sheet.html`.

The page is fully static: each mask is composited to cobalt, downscaled to
320 × 477, quantised to 16 colours and embedded as a PNG `data:` URI, so there
is no `<script>`, no CSS `mask-image` and no reference to `assets/`. It opens by
double-clicking the file and prints at three columns (`Ctrl+P`). Re-run it after
any change to the JSON or the masks:

`tools/build-prepositions-preview.py` writes the same page but appends the
batches that are drawn and not yet in `prepositions.json`, reading their PNGs
from the batch's folder under `assets/verb-propositions/` (archived batches keep
their own subfolder) and their rows from the batch plan. It imports the stock
builder for the shell, the CSS and the shipped cards, so the two sheets cannot
drift apart. Those cards have no example, build step or concept question yet, so
they show the gap instead of inventing the text, and each one carries a 64 px
strip with its contrast partner to check the pair.

Both write `assets/site/prepositions-sheet.html`, so the last one run wins: use
the preview while reviewing new art, the stock builder after a promotion.

Do not switch it back to CSS masks or linked image files: a failed mask load
hides the element, so a `file://` render comes out blank.

## What the pilot tests

## Definition of done for the pilot

- Thirty images at 512 × 763, cobalt ink on transparency, no text or numbers.
- Each image is readable at 64 px.
- A Dutch speaker can name the target sentence from the image alone, without the
  gloss.
- The contrast pairs are clearly different side by side, and neither image
  accidentally suggests the partner.
- The loop works without English: Ontdek → Kies het beeld → Klopt de zin? →
  Bouw de zin.
- The thirty images fit the six-minute session in `prepositions.md`.

## Not in this set

- `afhangen van` (hard to draw unambiguously at 64 px), `werken voor` (too
  close to `werken bij`) and `zoeken op` (separable `opzoeken`, a word-order
  item, not a frame).

- Audio. It is blocked by `decisions.md` open question 6.
- The noun `aandenken` ("souvenir"). It is a vocabulary card, not a frame. If it
  is wanted, it needs a souvenir-shop scene, not a preposition scene.
- A separate "wrong" version of any scene. The activity supplies the sentence;
  the art supplies the situation.

## Shared generation prompt

The prompt, negative rules and checklist are in `game-art.md`. Use that prompt
for every image, changing only the subject line to the scene above. This list
is the content spec; `game-art.md` is the style.

### One prompt for the first ten

> images: bold brush-pen sketch, cobalt blue (#2B50C8) only on plain white, wide
> contours with white interiors, most lines 4–8 px at 784 px wide, dense
> directional hatching for shadow, hair as the only filled mass. One idea per
> image. Adult proportions, profile or three-quarter view, focused neutral face
> with a brow, one eye, a nose line, a mouth and an ear; hands with a thumb and
> finger lines. The scene spans 90–100% of the width and the person 35–55%, with

> Netherlands; the drawing is a clue, not a cartoon. Leave the background flat

>
> 1. One person at a simple bus stop, looking at a watch. A blank sign on a
>    pole, maybe a bench. No bus arriving.
> 2. One person waiting outside a closed door, arms crossed or leaning on the
>    wall. A plain door with a handle, blank nameplate. No key, nobody entering.
> 3. A person gazing into space with a thought bubble containing a simple face.
>    No speech bubble, no question mark, no calendar.
> 4. A person at a table comparing two simple objects side by side, hand on
>    chin. Objects, not people.
> 5. A smiling person with a suitcase looking at a wall calendar with one day

> 7. Two people facing each other, talking, speech bubbles meeting. No object
>    between them, no phone.
> 8. Two people at a table with a simple house between them, speech bubbles
>    pointing at the house, one gesturing toward it.
> 9. A person stubbing out a cigarette in an ashtray, calm and determined. No

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
You have no file access. Do not ask to read any repository, document, image or
attachment. Everything you need is in this message.

TASK
Generate ten separate images for a Dutch practice game called Voorzetselpaden,
and nothing else. Each image is a wordless clue for one Dutch verb or adjective
plus a fixed preposition. The learner sees the image, recognises the everyday
situation, and connects it to the chunk. A Dutch speaker must be able to name
the situation from the drawing alone, without a caption. The Dutch and English
below are context for you only. None of those words may appear in the image.

STYLE — FOLLOW EXACTLY
- Bold brush-pen sketch in the hand of the Oefenpad logo: a wide-nib brush or
  chisel marker, thick pressure-varying strokes with dry-brush streaks and
  split bristles. Not pencil, fine-liner, flat vector, cartoon, stock,
  photorealistic, 3D or soft-shaded.
- Cobalt blue #2B50C8 only. No orange, red, green, second blue, grey, skin
  colour or full colour.
- Plain pure white background (#FFFFFF). No off-white, cream, beige or grey
  background. The white paper is intentional; it becomes transparency later.
  No gradients, soft shading, stippling, drop shadows, glow, blur, grain or
  paper texture. No border, frame, card, rounded rectangle or white plate.
- Contour plus hatching. Important edges are drawn twice, a few pixels off,
  and corners may stay open. Strokes taper: thinner at the ends, wider at the
  point of pressure. At 784 px wide: most lines 4–8 px, boldest contours
  9–14 px, hatching 2–4 px (at 1024 px wide: 5–10, 12–18, 3–5). Ink covers
  14–22% of the canvas, up to 27% for a scene with two figures and furniture.
- Hatching is wanted: quick, dense, directional strokes on the shadow side of
  folds and under objects, with white paper still visible between them. Never
  cross-hatch.
- Fill hair only, plus one or two small accents. Clothing, furniture and
  background stay white inside the contour. Never build the scene from filled
  silhouettes.
- One idea per image. The scene spans 90–100% of the width and the person
  35–55%; it may touch the left or right edge, with paper kept at top and
  bottom. Must still be nameable at 64 × 64 px.
- People have adult proportions, profile or three-quarter view, facing right:
  brow, one eye, nose line, mouth, ear, filled hair. Hands have a thumb and
  finger lines. No cartoon faces, open mouths or motion lines.
- Posture carries the meaning. The drawing is a clue for an adult learner,
  not a cartoon for children.
- No text, letters, numbers, words, logos, emoji, punctuation, arrows or
  readable signs anywhere. A sign in a scene must be blank. Blank speech
  bubbles are allowed as shapes, but they contain no letters, words or
  punctuation. Do not use a question mark.
- No decorative background: no plants, posters, wallpaper, shelves,
  landscapes or scenery that is not the idea.
- No culture-specific or Dutch souvenir imagery: no windmills, clogs, tulips,
  canals, cheese or similar. Everyday objects are fine.
- If the scene needs a caption to be understood, simplify or redraw it.

FORMAT
- Ten separate images, one per subject.
- 2:3 portrait, for example 1024 × 1536 px. All ten use the same camera, the
  same scale and the same line weight, because they sit side by side in one
  game.
- Raster PNG. Do not produce SVG code.
- No contact sheet, grid, collage or extra images. If you must return them one
  at a time, return them in the numbered order.
- Do not put the filename, a number or any label inside the image. Put the
  exact filename in the chat text above or below each image.

THE TEN SUBJECTS, IN ORDER

1. zeggen-tegen-persoon.png — Dutch chunk: zeggen tegen (to say to).
   Scene: two people close together; one leans in and says one short thing to
   the other, with a single small blank speech shape between them. The speaker
   is the clearest mark; the listener is calm and facing them.
   Must read: saying one short thing to someone.
   Avoid: a long story scroll (that is #2); a gift or object being handed
   over; two people arguing.

2. vertellen-aan-kind.png — Dutch chunk: vertellen aan (to tell to).
   Scene: one adult crouched or seated at eye level with a child, hands moving
   as if telling a longer story; a long blank ribbon or scroll shape rises
   between them. The child listens, chin up.
   Must read: telling a story to someone.
   Avoid: a single small speech shape (that is #1); a book with readable
   pages; a classroom or crowd.

3. praten-tegen-muur.png — Dutch chunk: praten tegen (to talk at).
   Scene: one person talking animatedly with open hands toward another person
   who has turned their back and is walking away. No speech bubble; posture
   does the work.
   Must read: talking at someone who is not listening.
   Avoid: two people facing each other and talking (that is the shipped
   praten met scene); a literal brick wall; a phone.

4. beschermen-tegen-regen.png — Dutch chunk: beschermen tegen (to protect
   against).
   Scene: one person standing dry and calm under a large open umbrella while
   rain slants down around them; the umbrella is the strongest silhouette.
   Must read: being protected from the weather.
   Avoid: a soaked person (that is #5); a second person; a sunny sky.

5. komen-door-regen.png — Dutch chunk: komen door (to be caused by).
   Scene: one soaked person, no umbrella, hair and clothes dripping, pointing
   up at a rain cloud as if naming the cause. The rain cloud and the wet
   person are the two masses.
   Must read: the rain is the cause.
   Avoid: an umbrella (that is #4); a person looking at a watch; a bus stop.

6. komen-uit-huis.png — Dutch chunk: komen uit (to come from).
   Scene: one person with a suitcase stepping out of the open door of a simple
   house, mid-stride, as if arriving from somewhere else. The doorway is the
   clearest mark.
   Must read: coming from a place.
   Avoid: a bus or car (that is stappen uit); rain; a person entering the
   house rather than leaving it.

7. kijken-door-sleutelgat.png — Dutch chunk: kijken door (to look through).
   Scene: one person bent toward a door, one eye close to a keyhole or a narrow
   gap, peering through. The door and the eye line are the main idea.
   Must read: looking through a small opening.
   Avoid: a window (that is #8); a telescope; a key in hand.

8. kijken-uit-raam.png — Dutch chunk: kijken uit (to look out of).
   Scene: one person standing at a window, hands on the sill or curtains
   pulled aside, looking out. The window frame is the clearest mark.
   Must read: looking out of a window.
   Avoid: a keyhole or door crack (that is #7); a person outside looking in;
   a landscape beyond the window.

9. doorgeven-aan-buur.png — Dutch chunk: doorgeven aan (to pass on to).
   Scene: two people on either side of a low fence or table; one hands a plain
   box or book across to the other, both hands visible. The object is plain,
   with no ribbon.
   Must read: passing something on to the next person.
   Avoid: a wrapped gift with a ribbon (that reads as blij met); a crowd; a
   telephone.

10. doorbrengen-met-vriend.png — Dutch chunk: doorbrengen met (to spend time
    with).
    Scene: two people relaxed side by side on a simple sofa; one reads a book,
    one holds a cup; a small plain wall clock without numbers. Both look
    comfortable, not busy.
    Must read: passing time together.
    Avoid: a party or celebration; a gift; a workplace; readable clock
    numbers.

CONTRAST PAIRS — DESIGN THESE TOGETHER
1 and 2 are a pair: same two figures, same camera, same distance. Change only
the speech shape — one small blob versus a long ribbon — and the listener's
posture.
4 and 5 are a pair: same rain, same camera distance. Change only the umbrella
and whether the person is dry or soaked.
7 and 8 are a pair: same person, same camera. Change only the opening — keyhole
versus window.
Draw each pair in the same sitting. At 64 × 64 px the two images must be
clearly different, and neither may suggest the other's chunk.
3, 6, 9 and 10 are singles; draw each one standalone. #3 must not repeat the
face-to-face composition of the shipped praten met scene.

VALIDATION BEFORE YOU FINISH
For every image:
- Downscale mentally or actually to 64 × 64: is the idea still nameable?
- Is it cobalt only, with no orange, no grey and no second blue?
- Is there any text, letter, number, logo, emoji, punctuation, arrow or
  readable sign? Remove it.
- Are the strokes tapered filled shapes, not uniform outlines?
- Is the background plain white, with no border, card, shadow or scenery?
- Does the scene span the frame without shrinking into a card, with the person 35–55% of the width?
Then check the pairs side by side. If either image in a pair suggests the
other's chunk, redraw it before delivering.

When finished, list the ten filenames and name any image whose 64 px
silhouette is still ambiguous. Do not add any image that is not on this list.

   tabletop. The object is the small mass.
   Must read: curious attention to a thing.
   Avoid: a book with readable pages; a sleeping posture; a crowd.

7. tevreden-zijn-met-resultaat.png — Dutch chunk: tevreden zijn met (to be
   satisfied with).
   Scene: one person stands back from a plain finished panel propped on a low
   stand, arms relaxed at the sides, head slightly tilted, a calm upward mouth
   line.
   Must read: satisfied with the outcome.
   Avoid: a thumbs-up; a crowd; a certificate.

8. bedanken-voor-de-uitnodiging.png — Dutch chunk: bedanken voor (to thank
   for).
   Scene: two people at an open doorway, one with a plain bag on the ground;
   that one holds out a flat open hand, palm up, in thanks, the other stands
   with a hand on the door frame. Both upright and smiling.
   Must read: thanking someone at the door.
   Avoid: a gift (that is #9); a handshake; a crowd.

9. feliciteren-met-de-verjaardag.png — Dutch chunk: feliciteren met (to
   congratulate on).
   Scene: the same doorway and the same two people, but the first now holds out
   a small plain wrapped box at chest height with both hands, and both lean in
   towards it. The box is the only difference that matters.
   Must read: congratulating someone with a gift.
   Avoid: a cake with candles; a card with letters; a crowd.

10. uitnodigen-voor-het-feest.png — Dutch chunk: uitnodigen voor (to invite
    to).
    Scene: one person holds out a plain blank card at chest height towards a
    second, who leans forward with one hand already reaching for it; an open
    doorway with empty space beyond stands behind them.
    Must read: asking someone to come.
    Avoid: a gift (that is #9); readable writing on the card; a crowd.

CONTRAST PAIRS — DESIGN THESE TOGETHER
8 and 9 are a pair: same doorway, same camera, same two figures. Change only
the object — an open empty hand in #8, a small wrapped box in #9. At 64 × 64 px
the box must be the obvious difference, and #8 must not contain a box.
1, 2, 3 are three different `uit` situations, but they are not a false-item
pair: draw them with the same scale, not the same composition, and make the
container (bus door, glass, bag) unmistakable at 64 px.
4–7 and 10 are singles. #4 is outdoors, alert and looking away; #5 is bent over
a bench; #6 is seated and curious indoors; #7 is standing back from finished
work; #10 holds a card out at a door. Keep all five visually distinct by
posture and object, not by shading.

VALIDATION BEFORE YOU FINISH
For every image:
- Downscale mentally or actually to 64 × 64: is the idea still nameable?
- Is it cobalt only, with no orange, no grey and no second blue?
- Is there any text, letter, number, logo, emoji, punctuation, arrow or
  readable sign? Remove it.
- Are the strokes tapered filled shapes, not uniform outlines?
- Is the background plain white, with no border, card, shadow or scenery?
- Does the scene span the frame without shrinking into a card, with the person 35–55% of the width?
Then check #8 and #9 side by side. If #8 could be read as "congratulating",
redraw it before delivering.

When finished, list the ten filenames and name any image whose 64 px
silhouette is still ambiguous. Do not add any image that is not on this list.

A lone person with a raised finger at a broken washing machine has nobody to complain to; it reads as boos over, which is row 24.

Add a listener who is not staff: the person points at the machine while speaking to a housemate. The appendix rows 76–78 already do this.

Appendix — V1 — wachten + denken (12 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Twelve separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. wachten-op-trein.png — wachten op (to wait for)
   Scene: person on a station platform, suitcase at their feet, looking down
   the empty track; the rails recede into the distance.
   Must read: waiting for a train to arrive.
   Avoid: standing outside a building (wachten voor); checking a watch; any
   departure board or text.

2. wachten-op-vriend.png — wachten op
   Scene: person at a cafe table with two cups, one untouched; they look
   toward the entrance, coat over the chair.
   Must read: waiting for a friend to arrive.
   Avoid: two people already talking (praten met); a gift.

3. wachten-op-eten.png — wachten op
   Scene: person seated at a table with an empty plate and cutlery, looking
   toward a kitchen door or serving hatch.
   Must read: waiting for food to arrive.
   Avoid: cooking (bezig zijn met koken); complaining about the food; a waiter
   already serving.

4. wachten-voor-winkel.png — wachten voor (to wait in front of)
   Scene: person standing outside a shop door, facing it with arms relaxed;
   shop interior visible through the glass.
   Must read: waiting in front of a shop.
   Avoid: entering the shop; waiting for a bus or train; looking at a watch.

5. wachten-voor-hek.png — wachten voor
   Scene: person standing outside a closed gate in a fence, facing the gate,
   hands on it or arms crossed; path beyond.
   Must read: waiting in front of a gate.
   Avoid: waiting for a person to arrive (no looking down the road); climbing
   the gate.

6. wachten-voor-kantoor.png — wachten voor
   Scene: person with a briefcase standing outside an office entrance, facing
   the closed door.
   Must read: waiting in front of an office.
   Avoid: working at a desk (werken bij); entering; a colleague greeting them.

7. denken-aan-huis.png — denken aan (to think of)
   Scene: person looking ahead, a thought bubble containing one simple house.
   Must read: thinking of home or a house.
   Avoid: two houses side by side (denken over); a real house in the room; a
   speech bubble with words.

8. denken-aan-eten.png — denken aan
   Scene: person looking ahead, a thought bubble containing one plate of food.
   Must read: thinking of food.
   Avoid: eating; a table with a real plate; several dishes.

9. denken-aan-vakantie.png — denken aan
   Scene: person looking ahead, a thought bubble containing a sun and a
   suitcase.
   Must read: thinking of a holiday.
   Avoid: a calendar with a marked day (uitkijken naar vakantie); packing a
   real suitcase; two destinations.

10. denken-over-twee-huizen.png — denken over (to think about, to consider)
    Scene: person seated, chin on one hand, two simple houses side by side in
    front of them; eyes moving between them.
    Must read: weighing two houses.
    Avoid: one house in a thought bubble (denken aan); a real estate agent; text.

11. denken-over-twee-autos.png — denken over
    Scene: person seated, chin on one hand, two simple car shapes side by side
    in front of them.
    Must read: weighing two cars.
    Avoid: driving; one car; a thought bubble.

12. denken-over-twee-reizen.png — denken over
    Scene: person holding two blank brochures side by side, one showing a
    simple sun and the other a simple mountain; comparing them.
    Must read: choosing between two trips.
    Avoid: packing; a calendar; text on the brochures.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- wachten op (1–3) vs wachten voor (4–6): op scenes show expectant arrival or
  service, with the person looking toward where the thing will come from.
  voor scenes show a person facing a building or barrier, waiting at that
  place. No op scene may look like standing outside a building; no voor scene
  may include a platform, track, suitcase or expectant gaze into the distance.
- denken aan (7–9) vs denken over (10–12): aan is one thing or person inside
  a thought bubble. over is two real alternatives in front of the person, with
  the person comparing them. No thought bubble in the over scenes; no second
  object in the aan scenes.
- 7 and 10 are a matched pair: one house in the mind versus two houses being
  weighed. Keep the same seated figure and camera.
- 8 is not zin in eten: there is no real plate and no eager reaching, only a
  thought bubble.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each
pair side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may
suggest the other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous
silhouette.

Appendix — V10 — kijken + doorgeven (9 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Nine separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. kijken-door-verrekijker.png — kijken door (to look through)
   Scene: person holding binoculars to their eyes, looking away.
   Must read: looking through binoculars.
   Avoid: a window (kijken uit); a telescope on a tripod is acceptable only if
   the handheld binoculars are unmistakable.

2. kijken-door-microscoop.png — kijken door
   Scene: person bent over a microscope, one eye at the lens.
   Must read: looking through a microscope.
   Avoid: binoculars; a magnifying glass.

3. kijken-door-kier.png — kijken door
   Scene: person peering through a narrow gap between curtains or a partly open
   door, one eye at the gap.
   Must read: looking through a crack.
   Avoid: a keyhole (existing scene); a window.

4. kijken-uit-treinraam.png — kijken uit (to look out of)
   Scene: person seated by a train window, chin on one hand, looking out; simple
   passing landscape lines beyond the glass.
   Must read: looking out of a train window.
   Avoid: binoculars; waiting for a train (wachten op trein); stepping out
   (stappen uit).

5. kijken-uit-tent.png — kijken uit
   Scene: person at the open flap of a tent, looking out; the tent opening
   frames them.
   Must read: looking out of a tent.
   Avoid: camping or relaxing; a window.

6. kijken-uit-balkon.png — kijken uit
   Scene: person leaning on a balcony railing, looking out over simple roofs.
   Must read: looking out from a balcony.
   Avoid: fear of heights (bang voor hoogte); waving.

7. doorgeven-aan-collega.png — doorgeven aan (to pass on to)
   Scene: two people at a desk, one passing a folder across to the other.
   Must read: passing a folder on.
   Avoid: a wrapped gift (blij met); signing a document.

8. doorgeven-aan-kind.png — doorgeven aan
   Scene: adult handing a toy or ball down to a child, the child reaching.
   Must read: passing something to a child.
   Avoid: a gift ceremony; throwing.

9. doorgeven-aan-medespeler.png — doorgeven aan
   Scene: runner passing a relay baton to a teammate, both in motion.
   Must read: passing the baton on.
   Avoid: a gift; a race finish.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- kijken door (1–3) vs kijken uit (4–6): door is looking through an instrument
  or a narrow opening, with the instrument or opening as the clearest mark. uit is
  a person inside an enclosure looking outward, with the enclosure framing
  them. 3 must not repeat the keyhole (existing scene). 4 is not waiting on the
  platform or stepping out of the train.
- 6 is calm looking, not fear of heights (bang voor hoogte).
- doorgeven aan (7–9) is an object moving hand to hand to another person, with
  both hands visible and no wrapping. 7 is not a gift (blij met); 9 is passing,
  not joining the game (meedoen met spel).

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V11 — doorbrengen + stappen + drinken (9 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Nine separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. doorbrengen-met-vrienden.png — doorbrengen met (to spend time with)
   Scene: three or four friends around a table playing a simple board game,
   relaxed, mid-laugh.
   Must read: spending an evening together.
   Avoid: a person pulling a chair in to join (meedoen met); one person
   isolated; a gift.

2. doorbrengen-met-oma.png — doorbrengen met
   Scene: younger person and an older relative sitting together over two cups
   of tea, both at ease; the older person talking.
   Must read: spending time with a grandparent.
   Avoid: caring for the older person (zorgen voor oma: no blanket, no helping
   hand); a telephone call.

3. doorbrengen-met-kind.png — doorbrengen met
   Scene: adult and child playing on the floor with simple blocks, both
   engaged and happy.
   Must read: spending time playing with a child.
   Avoid: watching over the child (letten op kind); feeding or dressing them
   (zorgen voor kind).

4. stappen-uit-auto.png — stappen uit (to step out of)
   Scene: person with one foot already on the pavement, hand on the open car
   door, rising out of the seat.
   Must read: getting out of a car.
   Avoid: standing in front of the car (wachten voor); a whole journey scene.

5. stappen-uit-trein.png — stappen uit
   Scene: person mid-step down from a train onto a platform, bag in one hand.
   Must read: stepping off a train.
   Avoid: waiting for a train (wachten op trein); already walking away on the
   platform (komen uit).

6. stappen-uit-boot.png — stappen uit
   Scene: person stepping from a small boat onto a wooden dock, one hand
   steadying on the boat edge.
   Must read: getting out of a boat.
   Avoid: falling into the water (vallen uit); sailing.

7. drinken-uit-kopje.png — drinken uit (to drink from)
   Scene: person holding a mug with both hands and drinking, eyes calm.
   Must read: drinking from a mug.
   Avoid: putting the mug down with a stop gesture (ophouden met drinken);
   pouring.

8. drinken-uit-fles.png — drinken uit
   Scene: person tilting a bottle to their mouth, head back slightly.
   Must read: drinking from a bottle.
   Avoid: pushing the bottle away (ophouden met); a baby bottle.

9. drinken-uit-beker.png — drinken uit
   Scene: person drinking from a simple paper cup, one hand.
   Must read: drinking from a cup.
   Avoid: a mug with a handle; a can; texting while drinking.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- doorbrengen met (1–3) is shared, easy time with a person, no task and no
  helping. 2 must not read as caring for the older relative (zorgen voor oma);
  3 must not read as supervising (letten op kind) or feeding (zorgen voor kind).
- stappen uit (4–6) shows the body in the act of leaving a vehicle, one foot
  placed and the vehicle edge under the hand. It is not komen uit (V9), which
  is a person already outside a place carrying something out. 5 must not
  suggest waiting on the platform. 6 is not vallen uit (V12): the person is in
  control, not tumbling.
- drinken uit (7–9) is a person actively drinking. None may look like
  ophouden met drinken (V2): no pushing away and no firm stop gesture.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V12 — vallen + letten + bezig (9 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Nine separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. vallen-uit-doos.png — vallen uit (to fall out of)
   Scene: an open cardboard box tipped on its side, a few simple objects
   spilling out onto the floor; no person needed.
   Must read: things falling out of a box.
   Avoid: someone handing objects over (doorgeven aan); a wrapped parcel.

2. vallen-uit-kast.png — vallen uit
   Scene: a cupboard door open, a stack of folded items and a cup tumbling
   out; no person needed.
   Must read: things falling out of a cupboard.
   Avoid: tidying or carrying a box (bezig zijn met opruimen); a closed door.

3. vallen-uit-bed.png — vallen uit
   Scene: person tumbling from a bed onto the floor, blanket pulled, startled.
   Must read: falling out of bed.
   Avoid: waking and stretching calmly (wakker worden); climbing in.

4. letten-op-hond.png — letten op (to pay attention to, to watch)
   Scene: person walking a dog on a leash, eyes fixed on the dog; alert but
   calm.
   Must read: keeping watch on the dog.
   Avoid: recoiling from a barking dog (uitkijken voor hond; bang voor hond);
   playing with the dog.

5. letten-op-pannen.png — letten op
   Scene: person standing at a stove, eyes on a pan, wooden spoon held but not
   stirring; watchful.
   Must read: watching the pan closely.
   Avoid: actively stirring and cooking (bezig zijn met koken); a burning pan.

6. letten-op-kind.png — letten op
   Scene: parent at a playground watching a child on a swing, eyes on the
   child, arms relaxed.
   Must read: keeping an eye on the child.
   Avoid: playing with the child (doorbrengen met kind); tending the child
   (zorgen voor kind).

7. bezig-zijn-met-koken.png — bezig zijn met (to be busy with)
   Scene: person at a stove stirring a pot, focused on the task, ingredients
   around.
   Must read: busy cooking.
   Avoid: merely watching a pan without stirring (letten op pannen); an empty
   table.

8. bezig-zijn-met-knutselen.png — bezig zijn met
   Scene: person at a table cutting paper and gluing pieces, hands active,
   offcuts around.
   Must read: busy with a craft project.
   Avoid: writing a report (werken aan verslag); looking at a finished piece
   (tevreden zijn met werk).

9. bezig-zijn-met-opruimen.png — bezig zijn met
   Scene: person carrying a box of household items across a half-tidied room,
   mid-task.
   Must read: busy tidying up.
   Avoid: finished and putting tools away (klaar met klus); a spotless room.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- vallen uit (1–3) is objects or a person leaving a container by gravity, with
  no hand passing anything and no control. 3 is not waking up.
- letten op (4–6) is sustained attention on a person or thing, hands not busy
  with the watched object. bezig zijn met (7–9) is active engagement in the
  task itself. Keep the same stove camera for 5 and 7: in 5 the person watches
  the pan without stirring; in 7 they stir and handle it. Neither may read as
  the other.
- 6 must not read as playing (doorbrengen met kind) or caring (zorgen voor
  kind). 8 must not read as writing a report; 9 must not read as having
  finished the job.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V13 — geinteresseerd + tevreden + uitnodigen (9 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Nine separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. geinteresseerd-in-boek.png — geinteresseerd in (interested in)
   Scene: person leaning over an open book, chin near the page, absorbed.
   Must read: absorbed in a book.
   Avoid: revising at a desk with pen and paper (klaar voor examen); a closed
   book.

2. geinteresseerd-in-schilderij.png — geinteresseerd in
   Scene: person in a gallery leaning toward a framed painting, studying it.
   Must read: interested in the painting.
   Avoid: painting it themselves (bezig zijn met knutselen); several paintings.

3. geinteresseerd-in-plant.png — geinteresseerd in
   Scene: person crouched to examine a plant closely, one leaf lifted, curious.
   Must read: examining a plant with interest.
   Avoid: watering or tending it (zorgen voor planten); a whole garden.

4. tevreden-zijn-met-eten.png — tevreden zijn met (satisfied with)
   Scene: person leaning back from a finished meal, hand resting on stomach,
   calm satisfied smile; empty plate.
   Must read: satisfied after the meal.
   Avoid: pushing the plate away in complaint (klagen over eten); still eating.

5. tevreden-zijn-met-huis.png — tevreden zijn met
   Scene: person standing in a living room, looking around with a settled,
   content expression, hands on hips.
   Must read: content with the home.
   Avoid: holding new keys and beaming (blij met huis); moving boxes.

6. tevreden-zijn-met-werk.png — tevreden zijn met
   Scene: person standing back from finished work with tools set down, arms
   folded, calm nod.
   Must read: satisfied with the finished work.
   Avoid: still working (bezig zijn met); celebrating over a gift (blij met);
   clearing up (klaar met).

7. uitnodigen-voor-eten.png — uitnodigen voor (to invite for)
   Scene: host at a set table gesturing with an open hand toward the chair,
   guest stepping in.
   Must read: inviting someone to eat.
   Avoid: waiting for the food (wachten op eten); already seated together.

8. uitnodigen-voor-wandeling.png — uitnodigen voor
   Scene: person at the door in a coat, gesturing outside toward a path, a
   second person approaching.
   Must read: inviting someone for a walk.
   Avoid: ready to leave alone (klaar voor vertrek); a finished walk.

9. uitnodigen-voor-spelletje.png — uitnodigen voor
   Scene: person holding out a board game box toward another who reaches for
   it.
   Must read: inviting someone to play a game.
   Avoid: a wrapped gift (blij met); a game already in progress (meedoen met
   spel); handing the box over as a gift (doorgeven aan).

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- geinteresseerd in (1–3) is curious attention leaning toward a thing, with no
  task and no care-taking. 3 is not zorgen voor planten; 2 is not a craft
  activity.
- tevreden zijn met (4–6) is a settled, low-energy contentment after something
  is complete. It is not blij met (V6), which is active joy over a new object;
  not klagen over (V7); not klaar met (V4), which marks the end of a task
  rather than the feeling about it. 4 has no complaint gesture; 6 has no
  tools in hand.
- uitnodigen voor (7–9) is one person offering an invitation with an open
  gesture toward an activity, the other still approaching. It is not wachten
  op eten (V1) or klaar voor vertrek (V4). 9 is an invitation, not a gift
  (blij met) and not joining a game already running (meedoen met spel).

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V14 — bedanken + feliciteren + eraan denken (9 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Nine separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. bedanken-voor-cadeau.png — bedanken voor (to thank for)
   Scene: person holding a wrapped gift with both hands, bowing slightly
   toward the giver, warm.
   Must read: thanking someone for a gift.
   Avoid: congratulating (feliciteren met); opening the gift alone; delight
   over a new object with no giver (blij met).

2. bedanken-voor-hulp.png — bedanken voor
   Scene: two people shaking hands warmly after a job, one nodding in thanks;
   a toolbox set down beside them.
   Must read: thanking someone for help.
   Avoid: congratulating on a job (feliciteren met baan); a gift.

3. bedanken-voor-eten.png — bedanken voor
   Scene: guest at a table inclining the head to the host after a meal, hands
   together; empty plates.
   Must read: thanking the host for the meal.
   Avoid: complaining about the food (klagen over eten); still eating.

4. feliciteren-met-baan.png — feliciteren met (to congratulate on)
   Scene: person enthusiastically shaking the hand of someone holding a blank
   contract, other hand on their shoulder, big smile.
   Must read: congratulating someone on a new job.
   Avoid: thanking for help (bedanken voor hulp); a job interview.

5. feliciteren-met-diploma.png — feliciteren met
   Scene: person congratulating someone who holds a rolled blank certificate,
   both smiling.
   Must read: congratulating on a diploma.
   Avoid: a gift exchange (bedanken voor); a graduation cap alone.

6. feliciteren-met-baby.png — feliciteren met
   Scene: two people leaning toward a small bundled baby, one with hands
   together and a joyful face.
   Must read: congratulating on a baby.
   Avoid: holding out a gift (bedanken voor); a christening scene.

7. eraan-denken-boodschappen.png — eraan denken (to remember to)
   Scene: person pausing mid-step, a thought bubble containing a shopping bag.
   Must read: remembering the shopping.
   Avoid: carrying real shopping bags; a list with words.

8. eraan-denken-sleutels.png — eraan denken
   Scene: person patting a pocket, a thought bubble containing a set of keys.
   Must read: remembering the keys.
   Avoid: searching under cushions (zoeken naar); keys in the hand.

9. eraan-denken-medicijn.png — eraan denken
   Scene: person pausing with a hand to the head, a thought bubble containing
   a simple medicine box.
   Must read: remembering to take medicine.
   Avoid: a doctor's visit (doktersbezoek); a real pill in the hand.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- bedanken voor (1–3) is gratitude after receiving something or help, with the
  giver present and the tone quiet. feliciteren met (4–6) is shared joy at
  someone else's good news, with a handshake or hands together and a big
  smile. Keep 2 and 4 apart with the same two-figure camera: 2 is a quiet
  thank-you after help, 4 is an excited congratulation.
- 1 is not blij met (V6): a gift is being received and thanked for, not
  admired as a new possession. 3 is not klagen over eten (V7).
- eraan denken (7–9) is an Ontdek-only card for the denken level: a person
  remembering a thing, shown only as a thought bubble, never scored as a
  contrast. It is not denken aan (V1): there the thought is about a person or
  place; here it is a task the person must not forget. No speech bubbles, no
  text. Give these three no `contrast` field.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Must read

Appendix — V2 — praten + ophouden (12 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Twelve separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. praten-met-buur.png — praten met (to talk with)
   Scene: two people leaning on either side of a low fence, facing each other,
   both with small speech shapes; relaxed.
   Must read: talking with a neighbour.
   Avoid: one person talking at the other's back (praten tegen); a topic object
   between them (praten over).

2. praten-met-collega.png — praten met
   Scene: two colleagues at a desk, turned toward each other, both gesturing;
   papers pushed aside.
   Must read: talking with a colleague.
   Avoid: working separately; one-sided speech.

3. praten-met-kind.png — praten met
   Scene: adult crouched to the child's eye level, both facing each other,
   small speech shapes in both directions.
   Must read: talking with a child.
   Avoid: an adult telling a long story (vertellen aan); scolding (boos op).

4. praten-over-film.png — praten over (to talk about)
   Scene: two people on a sofa facing each other, a blank screen between them,
   one gesturing at it.
   Must read: talking about a film.
   Avoid: watching the film passively; one-sided speech.

5. praten-over-probleem.png — praten over
   Scene: two people at a table with a broken cup between them, both looking at
   it and talking.
   Must read: talking about a problem.
   Avoid: repairing it (werken aan); complaining at a counter (klagen bij).

6. praten-over-vakantie.png — praten over
   Scene: two people with a map or brochure open between them, both pointing
   and talking.
   Must read: talking about a holiday.
   Avoid: packing; a calendar (uitkijken naar).

7. praten-tegen-lege-stoel.png — praten tegen (to talk at)
   Scene: person talking with open hands to an empty chair; no listener.
   Must read: talking at an empty seat.
   Avoid: a person in the chair (praten met); a phone.

8. praten-tegen-gesloten-deur.png — praten tegen
   Scene: person facing a closed door, talking with open hands; door shut.
   Must read: talking at a closed door.
   Avoid: knocking lines; a keyhole (kijken door).

9. praten-tegen-scherm.png — praten tegen
   Scene: one person talking animatedly at another whose back is turned and who
   is absorbed in a blank screen; no speech from the listener.
   Must read: talking at someone who is not listening.
   Avoid: two-way conversation; a phone call.

10. ophouden-met-drinken.png — ophouden met (to stop doing)
    Scene: person firmly pushing a bottle or glass away with one hand, the other
    hand raised flat in a stop gesture, resolved expression.
    Must read: stopping drinking.
    Avoid: drinking (drinken uit); finishing a task (klaar met).

11. ophouden-met-snoepen.png — ophouden met
    Scene: person closing a box of sweets and pushing it aside, flat hand on the
    lid, firm.
    Must read: stopping sweets.
    Avoid: eating; a gift.

12. ophouden-met-gamen.png — ophouden met
    Scene: person putting a game controller down on a shelf and stepping away,
    one hand still on it.
    Must read: stopping gaming.
    Avoid: playing; throwing it away.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- praten met (1–3) vs praten over (4–6) vs praten tegen (7–9):
  met is mutual, both face each other and both send speech. over is mutual too,
  but a topic object sits between the two and both refer to it. tegen is
  one-sided: the other person is absent, turned away, behind a closed door or
  absorbed in a screen, and only one person speaks. No met scene may contain a
  dominant topic object; no over scene may look like a plain chat; no tegen
  scene may show a listening, facing partner.
- ophouden met (10–12) is an active stop: the hand pushes, closes or puts the
  thing down. It is not finishing a task (klaar met) and not consuming the
  thing. 10 must not look like drinking (drinken uit).

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V3 — uitkijken + werken (12 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Twelve separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. uitkijken-naar-verjaardag.png — uitkijken naar (to look forward to)
   Scene: person smiling, holding a wrapped gift and a bunch of balloons,
   looking slightly up and forward.
   Must read: looking forward to a birthday.
   Avoid: a second person (feliciteren); a party already in progress.

2. uitkijken-naar-bezoek.png — uitkijken naar
   Scene: person setting a table for guests, two plates and cups, smiling and
   glancing toward the door.
   Must read: looking forward to visitors.
   Avoid: waiting for food (wachten op eten); a finished meal.

3. uitkijken-naar-reis.png — uitkijken naar
   Scene: person kneeling by an open suitcase, sun hat and folded clothes
   inside, smiling.
   Must read: looking forward to a trip.
   Avoid: a calendar with a marked day (existing vakantie scene); actually
   travelling; a thought bubble.

4. uitkijken-voor-hond.png — uitkijken voor (to watch out for)
   Scene: person stepping back, hands slightly raised, a barking dog in front.
   Must read: watching out for a dog.
   Avoid: fear (bang voor); petting the dog.

5. uitkijken-voor-gladde-vloer.png — uitkijken voor
   Scene: person walking carefully with arms out, looking down at a wet patch or
   puddle on the floor.
   Must read: watching out for a slippery floor.
   Avoid: mopping or cleaning; falling.

6. uitkijken-voor-fiets.png — uitkijken voor
   Scene: person at the edge of a bike path, one hand out, watching an
   approaching cyclist.
   Must read: watching out for a bicycle.
   Avoid: a car (existing scene); riding a bike.

7. werken-bij-bakker.png — werken bij (to work at)
   Scene: person behind a bakery counter, apron, arranging loaves of bread;
   simple shop.
   Must read: working at a bakery.
   Avoid: buying bread; working on a task (werken aan).

8. werken-bij-kantoor.png — werken bij
   Scene: person at a desk in an open office, another desk and a plant nearby,
   lanyard; focused.
   Must read: working at an office.
   Avoid: writing a report alone (werken aan verslag); a meeting.

9. werken-bij-winkel.png — werken bij
   Scene: person folding clothes or stacking shelves in a shop, apron; shop
   interior.
   Must read: working at a shop.
   Avoid: shopping; a customer.

10. werken-aan-fiets.png — werken aan (to work on)
    Scene: person kneeling beside an upside-down bicycle, tools in hand,
    repairing it.
    Must read: working on a bike.
    Avoid: riding; a bike shop counter.

11. werken-aan-verslag.png — werken aan
    Scene: person at a desk writing on papers or a laptop, focused; a single
    desk, no counter.
    Must read: working on a report.
    Avoid: reading for pleasure (geinteresseerd in boek); an open office with
    colleagues (werken bij).

12. werken-aan-tuin.png — werken aan
    Scene: person kneeling and digging in a garden bed with a trowel, plants
    around.
    Must read: working on a garden.
    Avoid: watering or care (zorgen voor planten); relaxing in the garden.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- uitkijken naar (1–3) vs uitkijken voor (4–6): naar is positive anticipation,
  smiling, with preparations, a gift or a calendar. voor is alert caution with
  a real hazard and no smile. No naar scene may contain a hazard; no voor scene
  may contain a celebration or packing.
- 1 is not feliciteren: the gift is held for a future event and no second
  person is present. 3 is not the existing vakantie scene: no calendar.
- werken bij (7–9) vs werken aan (10–12): bij shows a workplace and a role, with
  the person part of the place. aan shows a task or object in the hands, with
  no employer or counter. 8 shows the office around the person; 11 shows only
  the report. 12 is working, not watering (zorgen voor planten).

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

   Must read: finished the dishes.
   Avoid: still washing; a dirty pile.

2. klaar-met-huiswerk.png — klaar met
   Scene: student closing a book and pushing it aside, stretching, relieved.
   Must read: finished homework.
   Avoid: still writing (werken aan verslag); a teacher.

3. klaar-met-klus.png — klaar met
   Scene: person putting tools back into a toolbox beside a finished object.
   Must read: finished a job.
   Avoid: still working (werken aan); a professional workplace (werken bij).

4. klaar-voor-vertrek.png — klaar voor (ready for)
   Scene: person at the front door with coat on and bag in hand, ready to
   leave.
   Must read: ready to leave.
   Avoid: actually leaving (komen uit); waiting (wachten).

5. klaar-voor-examen.png — klaar voor
   Scene: student at a desk with pen and blank paper laid out, sitting upright.
   Must read: ready for an exam.
   Avoid: writing the exam; finished (klaar met).

6. klaar-voor-vergadering.png — klaar voor
   Scene: person at a meeting table with a folder and pen, upright, waiting for
   the meeting to start; empty chairs.
   Must read: ready for a meeting.
   Avoid: a meeting in progress; presenting.

7. vragen-aan-leraar.png — vragen aan (to ask a person)
   Scene: student with a hand raised, facing the teacher at the front; the
   teacher turned toward them.
   Must read: asking the teacher.
   Avoid: asking for information at a desk (vragen naar); asking for an object
   (vragen om).

8. vragen-aan-buur.png — vragen aan
   Scene: person at a neighbour's open door, speaking to the neighbour with a
   question gesture.
   Must read: asking a neighbour.
   Avoid: complaining (klagen bij); delivering something.

9. vragen-aan-arts.png — vragen aan
   Scene: patient seated and leaning toward a doctor, one hand raised in a
   question; the doctor listens.
   Must read: asking the doctor.
   Avoid: an examination; receiving medicine.

10. vragen-om-geld.png — vragen om (to ask for)
    Scene: one person holding out an open hand to another, who reaches for a
    coin or wallet.
    Must read: asking for money.
    Avoid: giving a gift; stealing.

11. vragen-om-advies.png — vragen om
    Scene: person with head tilted and hands open, asking another who listens
    thoughtfully; no object between them.
    Must read: asking for advice.
    Avoid: asking a factual question (vragen naar); a doctor.

12. vragen-om-pen.png — vragen om
    Scene: one person holding out an open hand toward another who offers a pen.
    Must read: asking for a pen.
    Avoid: writing; giving a gift.

13. vragen-naar-weg.png — vragen naar (to ask for information about)
    Scene: person holding a folded map, questioning another who points in a
    direction.
    Must read: asking the way.
    Avoid: asking for an object; holding out a hand for money.

14. vragen-naar-tijd.png — vragen naar
    Scene: person tapping their bare wrist where a watch would be, questioning
    another.
    Must read: asking the time.
    Avoid: a watch with readable numbers; a clock with numbers.

15. vragen-naar-adres.png — vragen naar
    Scene: person showing a blank card or paper to another, who points; both
    look at it.
    Must read: asking for an address.
    Avoid: handing over an object as a gift; text on the paper.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- klaar met (1–3) vs klaar voor (4–6): met is completion, with the task put away
  and a relieved posture. voor is preparation, with the person upright and the
  things for the event laid out. No met scene may look like readiness; no voor
  scene may look finished.
- vragen aan (7–9) vs vragen om (10–12) vs vragen naar (13–15): aan targets a
  person, om asks for a thing or favour, naar asks for information. 8 must not
  read as a complaint (klagen bij). 10 and 12 both use an open hand; money is
  a coin or wallet, a pen is a pen being offered. 13–15 must show information
  seeking (map, wrist, blank card), not an object being handed over.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V5 — zorgen + meedoen + zoeken + last hebben (12 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Twelve separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. zorgen-voor-hond.png — zorgen voor (to care for)
   Scene: person kneeling and putting a bowl down for a dog, or brushing it.
   Must read: caring for a dog.
   Avoid: playing; walking.

2. zorgen-voor-planten.png — zorgen voor
   Scene: person watering plants with a watering can, gentle posture.
   Must read: caring for plants.
   Avoid: gardening or planting (werken aan tuin); a florist.

3. zorgen-voor-oma.png — zorgen voor
   Scene: younger person placing a blanket over an older seated relative, or
   offering tea.
   Must read: caring for an elderly relative.
   Avoid: a purely social visit (doorbrengen met oma); medical treatment.

4. meedoen-met-gesprek.png — meedoen met (to join in with)
   Scene: person pulling a chair into a circle of two or three people already
   talking, leaning in.
   Must read: joining a conversation.
   Avoid: listening from afar; leading it.

5. meedoen-met-spel.png — meedoen met
   Scene: person joining a board game already in progress, taking a piece or
   sitting at the board.
   Must read: joining a game.
   Avoid: watching; winning.

6. meedoen-met-klas.png — meedoen met
   Scene: student moving a chair to a group table where others are working,
   sitting down.
   Must read: joining the class or group.
   Avoid: sitting alone; teaching.

7. zoeken-naar-bril.png — zoeken naar (to search for)
   Scene: person patting a tabletop and lifting cushions, peering around.
   Must read: searching for glasses.
   Avoid: wearing them; finding them.

8. zoeken-naar-hond.png — zoeken naar
   Scene: person in a park with a leash, calling and looking around; no dog
   visible.
   Must read: searching for a dog.
   Avoid: walking a dog (zorgen voor); a dog in view.

9. zoeken-naar-telefoon.png — zoeken naar
   Scene: person lifting a cushion and looking under a table; the phone is not
   visible.
   Must read: searching for a phone.
   Avoid: using a phone; finding it.

10. last-hebben-van-kou.png — last hebben van (to be bothered by)
    Scene: person shivering, arms wrapped around themselves, scarf and coat.
    Must read: bothered by the cold.
    Avoid: protecting against the cold (beschermen tegen kou); complaining to
    someone (klagen over kou).

11. last-hebben-van-hoofdpijn.png — last hebben van
    Scene: person pressing fingers to their temples, eyes closed, pained.
    Must read: suffering a headache.
    Avoid: thinking (denken); noise.

12. last-hebben-van-muggen.png — last hebben van
    Scene: person swatting at mosquitoes, annoyed; small insects around.
    Must read: bothered by mosquitoes.
    Avoid: anger at a person (boos op); sleeping.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- zorgen voor (1–3) is caregiving: feeding, watering, covering, offering. It is
  not affection (houden van) and not a social visit (doorbrengen met).
- meedoen met (4–6) is joining an activity already in progress: the person
  moves into the group or game. It is not already talking or playing with them
  (praten met, doorbrengen met).
- zoeken naar (7–9) is active search with the object absent. No scene may show
  the object being found. 8 is not walking the dog (zorgen voor hond).
- last hebben van (10–12) is discomfort caused by something. It is not a
  complaint spoken to another person (klagen over) and not protection against
  the cause (beschermen tegen). 10 must not look like 77 (klagen over kou),
  which is active complaint.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.

Appendix — V6 — blij + boos (12 images)

Grok-prompt, letterlijk
Same Voorzetselpaden house style as the delivered A0–A2 set. Twelve separate
images, 2:3 portrait, cobalt #2B50C8 only, brush line, plain white, no text or
numbers. Exact filenames, in this order:

1. blij-met-fiets.png — blij met (happy with)
   Scene: person beaming and hugging a new bicycle.
   Must read: happy with a bike.
   Avoid: riding it; being happy for someone else (blij voor).

2. blij-met-huis.png — blij met
   Scene: person in front of a simple house, holding up house keys, smiling.
   Must read: happy with a house.
   Avoid: moving in; thinking about houses (denken over).

3. blij-met-telefoon.png — blij met
   Scene: person holding a new phone and smiling at it.
   Must read: happy with a phone.
   Avoid: making a call; sad.

4. blij-voor-collega.png — blij voor (happy for)
   Scene: one person smiling and clapping for a colleague who holds a new
   bicycle; the bicycle belongs to the colleague, not the happy person.
   Must read: happy for a colleague.
   Avoid: the happy person holding the bike (blij met); a gift exchange.

5. blij-voor-buur.png — blij voor
   Scene: one person smiling for a neighbour who holds house keys in front of a
   house; the neighbour is the owner.
   Must read: happy for a neighbour.
   Avoid: the happy person holding the keys (blij met); a gift.

6. blij-voor-zus.png — blij voor
   Scene: one person smiling for a sister who holds a new phone; the sister is
   the owner.
   Must read: happy for a sister.
   Avoid: the happy person holding the phone (blij met); a gift.

7. boos-op-kind.png — boos op (angry at)
   Scene: parent standing over a child, frowning and pointing; the child looks
   down.
   Must read: angry at a child.
   Avoid: angry about a mess (boos over); hitting.

8. boos-op-hond.png — boos op
   Scene: person frowning and pointing at a dog beside a knocked-over object;
   the dog cowers.
   Must read: angry at a dog.
   Avoid: afraid of the dog (bang voor); caring for it.

9. boos-op-buur.png — boos op
   Scene: two neighbours facing each other, one gesturing angrily, the other
   defensive; no object between them.
   Must read: angry at a neighbour.
   Avoid: a fence and a friendly chat (praten met buur); complaining at a desk
   (klagen bij).

10. boos-over-rekening.png — boos over (angry about)
    Scene: person glaring at a blank bill in their hand, other hand on hip.
    Must read: angry about a bill.
    Avoid: anger at a person; paying.

11. boos-over-vertraging.png — boos over
    Scene: person at a platform, arms crossed, glaring at an empty track or a
    blank departure board.
    Must read: angry about a delay.
    Avoid: waiting for a train (wachten op trein); a person as the target.

12. boos-over-geluid.png — boos over
    Scene: person covering their ears and frowning beside a loudspeaker shape.
    Must read: angry about noise.
    Avoid: a headache (last hebben van hoofdpijn); a person.

CROSS-CHECKS — draw these together
- blij met (1–3) vs blij voor (4–6): met belongs to the happy person; voor
  belongs to the other person. 1↔4, 2↔5 and 3↔6 are matched pairs: same
  object, same camera, different owner. In the voor scenes the happy person
  does not hold the object and receives no gift.
- boos op (7–9) vs boos over (10–12): op has a person or animal as the target;
  over has a thing or situation as the target and no person to blame. 8 is
  anger, not fear (bang voor hond). 9 and 12 are a matched cause: a neighbour's
  noise versus the noise itself.

VALIDATION
For every image: at 64 × 64 the idea must still be nameable; cobalt only; no
text, numbers, arrows or readable signs; plain white; one idea. Check each pair
side by side: the two must remain clearly different and neither may suggest the
other chunk. Return only the listed files and name any ambiguous silhouette.
